what_it_does: Computers increasingly contain many specialized accelerator chips (for AI, graphics, encryption, etc.) alongside the main CPU, but those accelerators can access memory without the fine-grained safety checks the CPU applies. The standard isolation tool — an IOMMU (a translation unit that checks which memory pages a device may touch) — works only at the level of 4 KB pages and cannot stop an accelerator from accessing the wrong bytes within a page it is legitimately allowed to see. CHERI is a CPU architecture extension that attaches unforgeable bounds-and-permission tags to every pointer, giving software the ability to say 'this pointer may only access bytes 100–200 of this buffer.' CapChecker is a thin hardware shim placed between an ordinary, unmodified accelerator and the memory bus; it intercepts every memory request the accelerator makes, looks up the matching CHERI capability (the tagged, bounded pointer) that the CPU granted, and raises a fault if the access falls outside those bounds or violates the permission flags — all without changing the accelerator itself.
